name: Wei Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I think about this stuff a lot, so this is fun for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a general hand on a big warehouse build at the logistics park off the motorway. Mornings I'm usually helping the site engineer set out, banging in pegs and holding the staff while he reads the GPS. Afternoons it's whatever's needed: timber hoarding, cutting packers, making up the edge protection on the slab. I like the setting-out side because it's like a puzzle; I don't like being the one sent for the tea when the crane's down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you think about this stuff a lot. How do you use it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. I ask it to explain the drawings, I had it make me a revision plan for the setting-out course, and I use it to sort my budget, which is tight. I live with my girlfriend Sofia, she's a hairdresser, and we've got maybe two weeks saved. The warehouse jobs come and go round here; when this park's done there's nothing like it within an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm surprised, honestly, but fine. At work I'd still say the GPS kit is brilliant and that's not hype. Online I'd post something like, well, the tools are still useful, people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as is, which is mostly hands-on with a bit of screen. The real issue is that the logistics park finishes in a year and there's nothing big lined up. That's the same worry whether AI is a flop or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the setting-out course, because the engineer says he'll vouch for me. I'd keep using AI to study and budget. And I'd look at the next big project within commuting distance early, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit flat. Like a good film with a weak ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing big is lined up. How do you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I asked the AI to pull together the planning applications in the county. There's a solar farm and a school, and that's about it. A solar farm doesn't need many carpenters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no job turned up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agency work, or follow the engineer to his next site if he'll take me. Sofia's said she could move if it came to that. Her customers would follow her, she reckons, at least the loyal ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn the kit, not hide from it. At work I'd tell the lads the engineers will use AI for setting out and the ones who can help them will be kept. Online I'd post the free courses I find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's decent for me. Setting out is half thinking, half pegs in the mud, so if AI does the maths, they need someone who understands it on the ground. I'd be that person, if I move now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the setting-out course and ask to run the GPS rover on my own. I'd learn the AI planning tools the site office brings in, even unofficially. And I'd keep a small fund to buy my own used rover kit eventually, because freelancers get day rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a little nervous. Like the first day on a new site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kris, the older carpenter who does the hoarding. He refuses to use the tablet, he signs everything on paper. I'd try to show him, but he'd tell me to get lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's decent for you, but you have two weeks saved. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, fair. If they cut juniors while they figure out the new tools, I'm still a junior. I'd be relying on the engineer liking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, this is real. At work I'd say the setting-out maths goes to the computer by 2028 and the pegs go to robots by 2031. Online I'd probably post a plan for people my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. Everything I've been learning, the maths, the drawings, the AI does better by 2028. Then the hands-on part goes in 2031, and I'd be thirty-one with no trade and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd try to get hired by whoever sells the site robots, as the person who knows building sites. I'd use AI every day to learn the robot software. And Sofia and I would save hard and maybe move in with her parents for a year to bank the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I bet on the right horse and the race got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving in with Sofia's parents be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crowded. Her dad and I get on, but it's a two-bed flat. We'd do it for a year, maybe, to save six thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you in those three years between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The engineer probably goes before I do, which is mad. The thinking job goes first and the peg job lasts three more years. I'd be the last person on site who knows where the pegs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get your skills in order. At work I'd say learn the robots now. Online I'd post the steps I'm taking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five plus three gives me a real shot at the robot side. I could be a robot site technician by 2031, before the robots even arrive. That's ahead of the wave rather than under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do the setting-out course and start a robotics or surveying course part-time. I'd buy a used drone and get the licence, because drone surveys are already a job. I'd keep the warehouse job going while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Like having a head start in a race everyone else forgot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the drone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because sites already pay for drone surveys, and estate agents pay for house photos. If I can earn a bit on weekends, that's the savings fixed. A used one's about four hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk with this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spending four hundred I don't have. Sofia would say wait until we've saved a month first. She'd probably be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, don't waste it. At work I'd say the same. Online I'd say this is when you start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, thirteen years to robots on site feels great for me. I'd be forty with a surveying or drone business, maybe a van and a couple of rovers. That's a real career built on what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: finish setting-out, get the drone licence, do the weekend jobs. I'd keep the warehouse job for the steady money. I'd learn every AI tool surveyors use, because by 2036 I want to be the one running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little uneasy because ten years is still the same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the same ending mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One day, nothing I know will be worth paying for, and I'd be forty-ish, which is late to start again. But at least I'd have savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sofia say about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, but get a pension first. She's always the sensible one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. All my skills would be outdated before I'd finished learning them. What would help is a fast course on running site robots, paid while you learn, and a grant for kit like drones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my girlfriend's job. Hairdressing might be the safest job in our house. Nobody wants a robot cutting their fringe.
